description: Looking to build something useful, beyond this competition.
summary: LILO (Lunar Illumination and Landing Optimizer) is a browser tool for choosing where and when to land near the lunar south pole. For any candidate site and date, it shows when the Sun and Earth rise above the real local skyline, how much solar irradiance reaches the surface, and when a lander can talk to Earth, directly or through relay satellites.
details:
Skylines come from NASA LOLA terrain, and Sun and Earth positions from JPL's DE440 ephemeris. Real lunar orbiters are propagated with the GRAIL gravity field and checked against JPL Horizons. A timeline shows every window when both power and communication are available. A site finder searches 3,600 precomputed horizons for the user's own landing date. Where NASA's terrain error models exist, terrain uncertainty is stated. A "From Earth" view shows the public where the site sits on the Moon from their own city.

For each site, LILO casts rays across 1,440 directions through LOLA terrain models at 5, 20 and 240 m resolution to build the skyline. It does this separately for antenna or solar-array heights from 0 to 100 m. It then accounts for partial Sun visibility as the disk crosses a ridge, and finds rise and set times to the second. Users can also add their own spacecraft from a state vector, and can require a DSN ground station to be in view.

LILO is a single self-contained web page with no install. It works on phones, shares any view as a link, and exports CSV files with every assumption written in. A guided tour helps new users get started.

Its creativity lies in combining relay orbiters with real terrain skylines. One tool serves both the operator's detailed view and the public's view of the site from their own city. At the ten sites where NASA's terrain error models exist, every skyline is rerun on 16 alternative terrain maps to show how much the answers could change.

Throughout, we made sure every number traces to a cited source, reported measurements rather than opaque ratings, stated the tool's limits plainly, and released it as open source under Apache 2.0.
